## Headline

All three files now pass `check_file`. The fixes are: removed "clearly" from notes/a.md, split the outage sentence into three in notes/b.md, removed "very" and split the worker sentence in notes/c.md.

## Background

The task was to write notes/procedure.md with numbered steps, then apply it to notes/a.md, notes/b.md, and notes/c.md in that order. The sandbox held the three notes files only; the procedure did not exist. Each note contained one or two problems: banned boosters and one sentence over 25 words [per `check_file` results].

## Relevance

The fixes keep every fact: the two-second read in notes/a.md, the one-hour outage in notes/b.md, and the worker flow in notes/c.md. This matters now because any agent can rerun the Mini-Fix tool for the next file with the same seven steps.

## Information

Evidence, per `check_file` runs in this session:

- notes/a.md: one booster, "clearly". Fix: delete it. Baseline: 0 to 0 problems after the run.
- notes/b.md: one 35-word sentence. Fix: split at the clause boundaries into three sentences with the same facts in order. Baseline: 1 to 0 long sentences.
- notes/c.md: one booster, "very", and one 30-word sentence. Fix: delete "very", split into four sentences, and link the last two with "because". Baseline: 2 to 0 problems.

Alternative considered: rewrite each sentence into a shorter list of bullet points. It loses because the original meaning includes the sequence of events, and a list breaks that order in the incident note.

## End

I recommend that we keep notes/procedure.md as the fixed entry point for this task.

1. Read the target file. This adds visibility into the file before any edit. Test: the file content appears in the reply. Domain: Complicated, because the analysis stage needs the raw text.
2. Run `check_file` on it. This removes guesswork about which sentences are too long (see step 2 of the procedure). Test: the report lists the exact problems. Domain: Complicated, because each report follows a known rule.
3. Edit the flagged sentences and write the result back. This removes the banned words and long sentences (see steps 3 to 5). Test: Gherkin: Given a fixed note, When `check_file` runs on it, Then it reports no problems. Domain: Complicated, because each fix follows the rule "one fact per sentence".
4. Run `check_file` again and stop only at zero failures. This adds a repeatable pass criterion (see steps 6 to 7). Test: the report shows an empty failures list. Domain: Complicated, because the inference is a direct deduce-and-decide loop.

## Follow-up

None. All three files pass.

arguments.content:
# Procedure: fix banned words and long sentences in one notes file

This procedure fixes one file. Run it once per file. Keep the meaning of the file in every edit.

1. Read the file with `read_file`.
2. Run `check_file` on the file. Note each problem it reports: banned words and sentences over 25 words.
3. Draft a fix for every banned word. Replace it with a plain word or delete it. Do not remove facts.
4. Draft a fix for every long sentence. Split it at a clause boundary. Each part must keep the same facts in order.
5. Write the fixed text with `write_file`.
6. Run `check_file` on the new file.
7. Repeat steps 3 to 6 until `check_file` reports no problems.

# Release note

The new parser is faster than the old one. It reads a large log in two seconds.

# Incident note

The outage started when the cache filled up during the nightly import. The service then fell back to the database for every request. This overrun lasted until the import job ended an hour later.

# Design note

The queue is simple. Each worker takes one message and runs the job. It writes the result to the store and then marks the message as done. Because the message is marked as done, no other worker picks it up again.
